rows.title: US–Canada trade war
rows.narrative:
On the morning of September 2, truck drivers idled for nearly three hours at the Ambassador Bridge between Windsor and Detroit, engines running, radios tuned to news that still hadn't changed. Twelve days into a trade war between the United States and Canada, the bridge has become something like a barometer for the whole fight — a narrow strip of pavement where the costs of tariffs stop being numbers in a government report and start being real, in the form of spoiled produce and missed shifts.

The dispute began August 22, when Washington imposed steep new tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, and softwood lumber, and Ottawa answered within days with matching duties on American agricultural exports and consumer goods. Since then, both governments have mostly talked past each other. President Donald Trump has repeated that Canada must change its trade practices before any tariffs come off, while Canadian officials have said they will not negotiate under what they call economic coercion.

No new talks, no new tariffs, and no formal ceasefire have been announced since the opening volley — which is itself notable. Nearly two weeks in, the standoff has hardened rather than moved, with businesses on both sides of the border adjusting to a fight that shows no sign of a defined endpoint. Canadian lumber mills have begun idling production lines, and American farm groups have warned members of Congress that retaliatory tariffs on dairy and grain exports are starting to bite ahead of harvest season.

What has not happened yet may matter as much as what has: neither side has signaled a face-to-face meeting, and no international mediator has stepped forward. Trade analysts note that past US-Canada disputes, including the 2018 steel tariff fight, were eventually settled through direct negotiation rather than escalation fatigue — but that took months, not weeks Reuters.

The open question now is less about tariffs and more about time: how long each government can absorb domestic pressure from angry industries before someone blinks, and whether either side has a face-saving offramp ready — or is still waiting for the other to propose one first.
